title: Deep in one: Paul's letter to the Romans
subtitle: Sixteen sessions, one for each chapter of Romans: Paul's longest argument, from the guilt of the whole world to grace, the Spirit, Israel's future and a church of named friends.
intro: This track reads Paul's letter to the Romans a chapter at a sitting, sixteen sessions in all. Paul wrote it around AD 57, most likely from Corinth, to a church he had never visited, a mix of Jewish and Gentile believers in the capital of the empire. It is a letter, but it reads at times like one long argument, and its questions are the deepest ones: what is wrong with us, what God has done about it, and what kind of people that makes us.

Each session takes about fifteen minutes: read the chapter, then its notes in plain words, then come back to one question, one thing to do and one verse to keep. Romans has hard places where faithful Christians read Paul differently. The track sets out each reading in the form its own defenders would sign and leaves those questions open, while confessing plainly the gospel all of them share. Each session ends with a guide for a group.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through Deep in one: Paul's letter to the Romans. The group reads one chapter a meeting, sixteen in all. Romans is demanding, and it rewards a group that is willing to slow down, follow an argument and stay with a hard question for an evening without forcing it shut.

Each person reads the chapter, its notes and the session before the group meets. The meeting reads part of the chapter aloud and talks it over, using the group guide for that session, which is gathered below in order with the page each session opens and the question it asks.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten people is a good size, small enough that everyone speaks. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week, for sixteen meetings, and keep the end time you promised. A group that meets once a fortnight can take two chapters together where the argument runs on, such as chapters 9 to 11. A leader doesn't need to be a scholar. A leader needs to have read the chapter and its notes, and to be willing to say plainly when they don't know.

sections.title: The room
body: Sit where everyone can see each other, with the text open in front of everyone, in print or on a phone. Romans was written to be read aloud to gathered churches in Rome, most likely by the person who carried it. Ask a good reader to read the passage at each meeting, and let people take turns. Make it plain at the first meeting that anyone may pass on any question, that what people say about their own lives stays in the room, and that no one has to pray aloud.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Fifteen minutes: one person reads the heart of the chapter aloud while the others follow, then someone says in a sentence what Paul is arguing.
Thirty-five minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Ask where each answer is in the text.
Five minutes: one person reads the verse to keep, and the group says what it noticed in it.
Five minutes: the prayer prompt, in your own words.
Five minutes: name the next chapter and the page its session opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: Romans holds some of the most argued-over pages in the Bible: what Paul meant by works of the law, who the ‘I’ of chapter 7 is, how God chooses in chapter 9, what all Israel means in chapter 11, and how far chapter 13 binds anyone to a government. On each, the notes set out the readings without choosing, and so should the group. Give each view in the form its own defenders would sign, and don't settle for the group what the churches have not settled.

Keep two kinds of question apart. Whether we are justified by grace through faith in Christ, who died and was raised, is the ground every reading stands on. How election works, or who the ‘I’ is, divides faithful churches without dividing the faith. A group that can tell those apart can disagree on the second and still pray together on the first.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: Romans speaks of guilt, death, suffering and a self at war with itself, and some readers will hear their own life in it. When someone says so, stop and listen. Thank them, don't explain their suffering for them, and never hand anyone Romans 8:28 in fresh grief. Paul does not call suffering good. He says nothing can separate us from God's love.

Some passages have been misused to wound people: chapter 1 turned into contempt for gay neighbours, chapter 13 used to demand silence under injustice, chapter 12 used to keep someone where they are being harmed. The notes refuse every one of those uses, and so should the group. If someone says that anyone is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has become too heavy to set down: guilt or fear that will not let them rest, an addiction they cannot break, grief that has taken their sleep or appetite for weeks, harm done to them at home or in a church, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor.

sessions.title: Not ashamed of the gospel
teaching: Paul introduces himself to a church he has never met, and in two verses he states the theme of the whole letter: the gospel “is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek” (Romans 1:16). In it the righteousness of God is revealed. The rest of Romans works that sentence out. Notice that the gospel is first something about God, his Son descended from David and declared by the resurrection, before it is anything about us.

Then Paul turns to the dark. From verse 18 he describes the human race pushing away a truth it could see in creation and exchanging the glory of God for images of created things. Three times he says God gave them over to what they wanted. The list of what follows ends with envy, gossip and disobedience to parents, so that no reader stands outside it. The notes take up the hard verses, including those on same-sex relations, and set out how Christians read them.

open.label: Romans 1, passage by passage
open.why: Paul's greeting, the theme of the letter, and the exchange of God's glory for idols, each passage explained in plain words with its hard questions.

also.label: Romans in the Study Bible
also.why: Who wrote Romans, when, from where and to whom, how the argument is built, and why it has mattered so much in the church's history.

also.label: The letter to the Romans
also.why: The whole letter in short pictures, so you can see the shape of the argument before you read it a chapter at a time.

also.label: The cities of Paul
also.why: What Rome was like in the 50s, who the believers there were, and why a letter to a city Paul had never visited looks the way it does.

sessions.question: Paul says the problem behind every other wrong is worshipping something created in place of the Creator. What do you trust in the place where God belongs?
sessions.do: Read Romans 1:1-17 and underline everything Paul says about God and his Son before he says anything about people. Then read 1:18-32 and mark the three times God gave them over.

verse.text: I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek.

care: If you are gay, or love someone who is, you are met with respect here. If these verses weigh on you, talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is a letter you have received that you have kept, and why did you keep it?
discuss: Paul says he is not ashamed of the gospel. Why might anyone in Rome, or anywhere today, be tempted to be?
Paul says people exchanged the glory of God for images. What do people exchange it for now?
The list at the end of the chapter includes gossip and envy. Why do you think Paul made sure it reached everyone?
group.pray: Give thanks for the gospel as God's own power and not a human idea, and ask that each person would see their own idols this week without despair.

sessions.title: The judge who is judged
teaching: Chapter 1 ended with a list that a respectable reader might have nodded along to. Chapter 2 turns on that reader at once: “You, therefore, have no excuse, you who pass judgment on another” (Romans 2:1). This is the move of the prophet Nathan with King David, letting a man condemn a stranger and then telling him he is the man. God will judge each person by their deeds, Paul says, and he shows no favouritism. Gentiles who never had the law still show its work written on their hearts.

Then Paul speaks to a fellow Jew who rests in the law and boasts in God, and asks whether the teacher of others teaches himself. Paul is a Jew writing about his own people, not an outsider sneering, and his point reaches every religious insider. Being near the law, or the church, is not the same as keeping it. What counts is a circumcision of the heart, by the Spirit.

open.label: Romans 2, passage by passage
open.why: You who pass judgment, judgment by deeds, the law written on the heart and circumcision of the heart, each explained in plain words.

also.label: Judgment in the Study Bible
also.why: What the whole Bible says about God as judge, so you can read Paul's warnings beside the prophets and the words of Jesus.

also.label: What honour and shame meant
also.why: Paul writes about boasting and praise to people raised on honour and shame, and this guide shows how that world heard him.

sessions.question: Paul says God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance. Where have you treated God's patience as permission instead?
sessions.do: Think of one person or group you find it easy to judge. Read Romans 2:1-4 slowly with that person in mind, and write down honestly where the same thing lives in you.

verse.text: Or do you disregard the riches of His kindness, tolerance, and patience, not realizing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: When have you criticised someone for something and then caught yourself doing it?
discuss: Paul lets the reader agree with chapter 1 before turning on them. Why is that more effective than starting with an accusation?
Paul says God shows no favouritism. Which kinds of favouritism do religious people most expect from God?
What would a circumcision of the heart look like in a church that has every outward mark of faith?
group.pray: Ask God to show each person where they judge others for what they excuse in themselves, and give thanks that his kindness is patient.

sessions.title: But now: righteousness from God
teaching: Paul closes his case with a chain of psalms, “There is no one righteous, not even one” (Romans 3:10), and then two words change everything: but now. A righteousness from God has been revealed apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe, “for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:23-24). God set Christ forth as an atoning sacrifice, so that he is both just and the one who justifies.

What does Paul mean when he says no one is justified by works of the law? The Reformation reading, from Luther and Calvin, says Paul rules out every human effort offered to earn standing with God. The New Perspective, named by James Dunn in 1982 and built on E. P. Sanders's 1977 study of Judaism as a religion of grace, says Paul means chiefly the marks that set Jews apart from Gentiles, such as circumcision and food laws, and that his target is a people defined by them. Each points to verses the other must explain. Both confess that we are justified by grace through Christ.

open.label: Romans 3, passage by passage
open.why: God's faithfulness, no one righteous, the righteousness of God through faith and what the cross did, with the readings set out plainly.

also.label: Justification in the Study Bible
also.why: What it means to be declared right with God, traced through the whole Bible, with how the traditions have understood it.

also.label: The atonement in the Study Bible
also.why: The pictures Scripture uses for what the cross achieved, sacrifice, ransom, victory and substitution, and how they fit together.

also.label: The Reformation
also.why: How a monk's reading of Romans helped split the Western church in the sixteenth century, told fairly from more than one side.

sessions.question: Paul says all have sinned and are justified freely. Which half of that sentence is harder for you to believe about yourself?
sessions.do: Read Romans 3:21-26 aloud and write down every word that describes what God has done. Then count how many describe what we do.

verse.text: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is the best gift you have received that you could never have paid for?
discuss: Why does it matter to Paul that God is both just and the one who justifies, and not only merciful?
State the Reformation reading of works of the law and the New Perspective as their defenders would. What does each see clearly?
Paul says boasting is excluded. Where does boasting still creep into how Christians think about themselves?
group.pray: Give thanks in your own words that God justifies freely by grace, and pray for anyone who still believes they must earn their place.

sessions.title: Abraham believed God
teaching: Paul knows the objection a Jewish reader would raise: what about Abraham, our father? So he goes to Genesis. “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Romans 4:3). That sentence comes in Genesis 15, years before Abraham was circumcised in Genesis 17. So Abraham is the father of all who believe, the uncircumcised as well as the circumcised. The promise rested on grace from the start, which is why it can reach everyone.

Then Paul shows what that faith was like. Abraham was about a hundred years old and Sarah past bearing children. He faced the facts squarely, Paul says, and still trusted the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being things that do not exist. Faith here is not a feeling or a leap away from evidence. It is trust in a particular God who keeps his word, and Paul says the same God raised Jesus from the dead.

open.label: Romans 4, passage by passage
open.why: Abraham credited, David's blessing, faith before circumcision and hope against hope, each passage explained in plain words.

also.label: Abraham in the Bible's story
also.why: Where Abraham stands in the whole story of Scripture, from the call out of Ur to the promise that all nations would be blessed through him.

also.label: Faith in the Study Bible
also.why: What the Bible means by faith, traced from Abraham to Hebrews 11, so that trust is not confused with wishful thinking.

sessions.question: Abraham faced the facts of his body and still trusted God's promise. What fact in your life makes trusting God hardest?
sessions.do: Read Genesis 15:1-6 and then Romans 4:18-25. Write down what Abraham had to go on, and what you have to go on that he did not.

verse.text: He was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification.

care: If you have prayed for someone to be rescued, from illness, from danger, from prison, from death, and the rescue did not come, this chapter does not say your prayer was too weak. The three friends in Daniel said God was able to deliver them, “But even if He does not” (Daniel 3:18), they would still trust him. Grief and confusion at such a loss are not a lack of faith. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who in your life kept a promise to you when it would have been easier not to?
discuss: Why does it matter so much to Paul that Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised?
Paul says Abraham faced the facts without weakening in faith. How is that different from ignoring the facts?
Paul says God justifies the ungodly. Why is that phrase offensive, and why is it good news?
group.pray: Give thanks for the God who gives life to the dead, and pray for anyone in the group waiting on a promise that seems impossible.

sessions.title: Peace with God, and two men
teaching: Chapter 5 begins with what justification brings: peace with God, access to grace and a hope that does not disappoint. Paul even says suffering can produce endurance and character, though never that suffering is good. Then he names the measure of God's love: “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). God did not wait for anyone to improve.

From verse 12 Paul sets two men side by side. Through Adam sin entered the world, and death through sin. Through Christ comes the gift, which is not like the trespass but far greater. Christians have read the link with Adam differently. Augustine, reading a Latin text that said all sinned in Adam, taught that the whole race shares Adam's guilt. Eastern Orthodox Christians have generally read it as death passed to all, so that each of us, born mortal, sins in turn. Both hold that everyone needs the second Adam, and that where sin increased, grace increased more.

open.label: Romans 5, passage by passage
open.why: Peace with God, Christ dying for the ungodly, and sin and death through one man set against the gift through another, explained plainly.

also.label: Sin in the Study Bible
also.why: What Scripture means by sin, from Eden onward, and how the traditions have understood what we inherit from Adam.

also.label: The fall in the Bible's story
also.why: The garden, the first disobedience and its long shadow, the part of the story Paul is reading when he speaks of one man.

sessions.question: Paul says Christ died for us while we were still sinners. Do you believe God loves you as you are now, or as you hope to become?
sessions.do: Read Romans 5:12-21 and make two columns, one headed Adam and one headed Christ. Write under each what came into the world through him.

verse.text: But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

care: If you are suffering now, your pain is real, and you are not failing God by feeling it. The psalms are full of people who cried out to God. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). Please do not carry it alone: talk to someone you trust, a friend, a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. The site's Honest Answer, ‘If God is good, why is there so much suffering?’, faces the larger question.

group.open: What would it be like to have no one left who was angry with you?
discuss: Paul says suffering can produce character, and the notes warn against handing that to someone in fresh pain. Why are both needed?
How do Augustine's reading of Adam and the Eastern reading differ, and what do they share?
Paul says grace increased all the more where sin increased. What could someone wrongly conclude from that?
group.pray: Give thanks for peace with God through Christ, and pray for anyone you know who believes they must become better before God will have them.

sessions.title: Dead to sin, alive to God
teaching: Paul has just said that grace outruns sin, and he hears the obvious question: shall we go on sinning so that grace may increase? His answer is not a new rule but a new identity. Those baptised into Christ were baptised into his death, buried with him, so that as he was raised they might walk in newness of life. A dead man is free from the master who owned him. Paul tells believers to count themselves dead to sin and alive to God, and to stop offering their bodies to a master they no longer belong to.

Then he puts it as a choice between two kinds of slavery. Everyone serves something. One master pays wages and the other gives a gift, and Paul sets them side by side in one sentence. Baptism is here as the picture of union with Christ, and churches differ on who should be baptised and what it does, a question the notes leave open. What none of them doubts is the union itself.

open.label: Romans 6, passage by passage
open.why: Shall we go on sinning, baptised into his death, dead to sin and alive to God, and two masters, each explained plainly.

also.label: Union with Christ in the Study Bible
also.why: What it means to be in Christ, the phrase Paul uses more than any other, traced through his letters and the Gospel of John.

also.label: Baptism and the Supper
also.why: Short pictures of the two signs Jesus gave his church, what they show and where Christians differ about them.

sessions.question: Paul says everyone serves some master. What would the people closest to you say you serve?
sessions.do: Read Romans 6:11-14 each morning this week. Each evening, write down one moment when you acted as someone who no longer belongs to the old master.

verse.text: For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is a habit you once had that has no hold on you now, and how did it lose its grip?
discuss: Paul answers the question about sinning more with who you are, not with a rule. Why might that work better?
If you were baptised, what do you remember of it, and does Paul's picture of burial and rising change how you see it?
Wages are earned and a gift is not. Why does Paul set death and life in those two different terms?
group.pray: Pray for freedom from whatever still acts like a master in each life, and give thanks that in Christ it no longer owns you.

sessions.title: The law, and a divided self
teaching: Is the law the problem, then? Paul says no. The law is holy and good, but sin took the commandment and used it as a foothold, so that the very word meant for life became the occasion of death. Then comes the passage people remember: a self that delights in God's law and keeps doing what it hates, ending in a cry, “What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24).

Who is this ‘I’? Augustine in his later writings, followed by Luther, Calvin and much of the Lutheran and Reformed tradition, hears a believer's present struggle, pointing to the present tense and the delight in God's law. Many early writers and many modern scholars hear a person under the law without the Spirit, since chapter 6 says believers are free and the Spirit is not named here. Others hear Paul speaking in character for Adam or for Israel. On every reading the law is good, sin is the problem and rescue comes through Jesus Christ.

open.label: Romans 7, passage by passage
open.why: Free from the law, the commandment and the deceiver, and the struggle of verses 14 to 25, with the readings set out fairly.

also.label: The law in the Study Bible
also.why: What God's law was for, from Sinai to the Sermon on the Mount, and how the New Testament speaks of it after Christ.

also.label: Sanctification in the Study Bible
also.why: How Scripture speaks of growing in holiness, which bears on whether Romans 7 describes the Christian life now.

sessions.question: Whichever reading of the ‘I’ you hold, where do you recognise yourself in verses 14 to 25?
sessions.do: Read Romans 7:14-25 aloud and stop after verse 24. Wait a moment before reading verse 25. Write down what changes between the cry and the thanks.

verse.text: What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord!

care: If you are worn down by failing again and again, or caught in an addiction you cannot break, you are not alone, and you are not beyond help. Paul's cry was answered with thanks. Please talk to someone: a doctor, a pastor, a counsellor, or a group that helps people with what you are facing. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: When have you known exactly what you should do and still not done it?
discuss: Set out the reading of the ‘I’ as a believer's struggle and the reading of a person under the law, each as its holders would. Which verses press hardest on each?
Paul insists the law is good even though sin used it. Why does it matter to him not to blame the law?
The cry of verse 24 asks who, not what. Why is the answer a person rather than a method?
group.pray: Bring before God in your own words whatever you keep doing that you do not want to do, and give thanks that the cry in this chapter was answered.

sessions.title: No condemnation, and no separation
teaching: Chapter 8 opens with “Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1), and the Spirit, hardly named so far, now fills the chapter. What the law could not do, God did by sending his Son. The Spirit gives life, makes believers children who cry Abba, Father, and joins their groaning to the groaning of a whole creation waiting to be set free. When we don't know what to pray, the Spirit intercedes.

Verse 28 is much loved and often misused. The ‘all things’ include the famine and sword named a few verses later, and Paul does not call them good. He says they cannot defeat God's purpose, which is to make us like his Son. Churches read verses 29 and 30 on foreknowing and choosing in different ways. Then the chapter ends with a list of everything that might come between us and God's love, death and life, angels and powers, the present and the future, and says that none of it can.

open.label: Study Romans 8 step by step
open.why: The guided walk takes you through the chapter in seven steps, so that you see what Paul says before you read what anyone says about it.

also.label: Romans 8, passage by passage
also.why: No condemnation, Abba Father, creation groaning, all things working together and nothing able to separate, each explained in plain words.

also.label: Romans 8:28
also.why: A short film that sets the much-quoted verse back in its chapter, so it is heard as Paul meant it and not as a slogan.

also.label: Does Romans 8:28 mean everything happens for a reason?
also.why: What the verse promises and what it does not, read in its own chapter and in the world its first hearers lived in.

sessions.question: Paul lists everything that might separate you from God's love and says none can. Which item on his list do you most fear?
sessions.do: Read Romans 8:31-39 aloud slowly. Then write your own list of what you fear could come between you and God, and read verses 38 and 39 over it.

verse.text: For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

care: If you are afraid that you have lost God's love, read verses 38 and 39 slowly. That fear is not usually the mark of someone who has fallen away. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

What if ‘Father’ is a hard word for you? Some readers had a father who was absent, or who hurt them. If your own father was not there, or did not show you love, this verse is not asking you to picture him. It is telling you what you should have been shown, and what God is. God's love as a Father is not limited by the father you had. A psalm says, “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me” (Psalm 27:10). If what happened to you still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: If you are willing to say, has anyone ever quoted a Bible verse to you that helped, or one that hurt?
discuss: No condemnation comes first and the call to live by the Spirit comes after. Why does that order matter?
Paul says creation itself groans. What does that do to the idea that Christianity is only about saving souls?
How would you speak about verse 28 to someone in fresh grief, now that you have read the whole chapter?
group.pray: Give thanks that nothing can separate you from the love of God in Christ, and pray for anyone you know who is groaning and cannot find words.

sessions.title: God's word has not failed
teaching: Chapter 9 begins with grief. Paul says he has deep sorrow for his own people, Israel, most of whom have not believed in their Messiah, and he could wish himself cut off for their sake. Then he asks whether God's word has failed, and answers from Israel's own story: Isaac and not Ishmael, Jacob and not Esau, mercy on whom God has mercy, Pharaoh hardened, the potter and the clay.

This is among the most argued-over chapters in the Bible, and the notes set out three readings. The Reformed reading holds that God chooses before birth those he will save, out of free mercy. The Arminian and Wesleyan reading stresses God's patience with the vessels of wrath and holds that his choosing rests on his knowing who will believe, or on his choice of all who are in Christ. A corporate reading says Paul speaks of peoples and their roles in God's plan rather than each person's destiny. Each is held by faithful Christians. All agree that salvation begins in God's mercy and not in our effort.

open.label: Romans 9, passage by passage
open.why: Paul's grief, Isaac and Jacob, mercy and Pharaoh, the potter and the clay, with the readings of election set out without choosing.

also.label: Does God choose us, or do we choose him?
also.why: The case on each side of the old question, stated so its own holders would recognise it, and what both sides agree on.

also.label: Election in the Study Bible
also.why: What the whole Bible says about God's choosing, from Abraham and Israel to the church, with how the traditions read it.

also.label: Where Christians differ
also.why: The questions that divide faithful churches without dividing the faith, set side by side, so that chapter 9 is read in good company.

sessions.question: Paul argues about election with tears for his own people. What happens when the doctrine is discussed without the grief?
sessions.do: Read Romans 9:1-5 before anything else in the chapter, and write down the eight gifts Paul says belong to Israel. Then read the rest, holding that list in mind.

verse.text: So then, it does not depend on man’s desire or effort, but on God’s mercy.

care: If you are afraid that you are not chosen, read 8:38-39 slowly. That fear is not usually the mark of someone God has turned away. Paul's own invitation stands open: “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13). Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who is someone you love who does not share your faith?
discuss: State the Reformed reading and the Arminian reading of this chapter as each side would put it. What does each protect?
Paul asks who we are to talk back to God, yet he spends three chapters wrestling openly. How do those fit together?
Where in your own church have different views on election made it hard to stay together, and what helped?
group.pray: Pray by name for people you love who do not believe, with Paul's sorrow and his hope, and give thanks that salvation rests on God's mercy.

sessions.title: The word is near you
teaching: Paul holds two things together in chapter 10. Israel, he says, has a zeal for God that is not based on knowledge, seeking a righteousness of its own, and “Christ is the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4). Readers differ on whether end means goal or stop, and many hear both. Then he quotes Moses: the word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart. Salvation is not up in heaven to be fetched down. It is confessing that Jesus is Lord and believing that God raised him from the dead.

Confessing Jesus as Lord was not a private sentiment in Rome, where the same title was given to Caesar. And the call goes to everyone, because there is no difference between Jew and Greek. Then Paul asks how anyone will call on one they have not believed, or believe without hearing, or hear without someone sent. The chapter ends with God holding out his hands all day to a people who resist.

open.label: Romans 10, passage by passage
open.why: Zeal without knowledge, Christ the end of the law, confess and believe, and how they will hear, each explained in plain words.

also.label: What gospel and Lord meant under Caesar
also.why: The words Paul uses were already in use for the emperor, and this guide shows what it meant to say them of Jesus in Rome.

also.label: What about those who never heard?
also.why: Paul asks how they will hear without a preacher. This answer takes up the question that follows, with the views set out honestly.

sessions.question: Paul says the word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart. What would it mean for you to say Jesus is Lord and mean every word?
sessions.do: Write down the name of one person who has never heard the gospel from anyone who loves them. Pray for them by name each day this week, and look for one honest conversation.

verse.text: that if you confess with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved.

care: If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who was the first person who told you about Jesus in a way you actually heard?
discuss: Paul says Israel had zeal without knowledge. Where can zeal for God run ahead of knowing him today?
Jesus is Lord was a political claim in Rome. What does it claim against the powers you live under?
Paul's chain of questions ends with someone being sent. Who has been sent to you, and to whom might you be sent?
group.pray: Pray by name for people who have not heard, and ask that each person in the group would be ready to speak when the time comes.

sessions.title: The olive tree, and the depth of God
teaching: Has God rejected his people, then? Paul, an Israelite himself, says by no means. There is a remnant chosen by grace, and Israel's stumble is not a fall; through it salvation has come to the Gentiles, to make Israel jealous. Then he gives the Gentile believers in Rome a picture: an olive tree whose natural branches were broken off, with wild branches grafted in. Do not boast, he tells them. You do not support the root; the root supports you.

Then comes the sentence that all Israel will be saved. Many read it as a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before the end. Others read all Israel as the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile together, or as every Jewish believer across history. The notes don't choose, and they make no claim about any modern state. On any reading God's gifts and call are irrevocable, and Paul stops arguing and breaks into praise at the depth of God's wisdom.

open.label: Romans 11, passage by passage
open.why: The remnant, a stumble and not a fall, the olive tree, all Israel saved and the doxology, with the readings set out without choosing.

also.label: Israel in the Study Bible
also.why: What Scripture says about Israel as God's people, from Abraham to Paul, and how the church has understood its own relation to Israel.

also.label: Cross-references
also.why: Follow the verses Paul quotes from Isaiah, Deuteronomy and the Psalms in these chapters back to where they first stood.

sessions.question: Paul warns Gentile believers not to boast over the branches broken off. What does the church owe to Israel?
sessions.do: Read Romans 11:33-36 aloud as a prayer. Then write down one question about God you have not been able to answer, and set it under those verses.

verse.text: O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways!

group.open: What is something you were given that you only later realised you could never have earned?
discuss: The olive tree has one root and branches of two kinds. What does that picture say against Christian contempt for the Jewish people?
Set out the readings of all Israel will be saved as their holders would. What do they share?
Paul ends three chapters of argument in praise rather than a conclusion. What does that teach about how to hold hard questions?
group.pray: Give thanks for the root that supports the church, pray for the Jewish people with love, and praise God in your own words for what you cannot fathom.

sessions.title: Living sacrifices
teaching: Chapter 12 begins with therefore, and everything Paul has argued now becomes a way of life. In view of God's mercies, offer your bodies as living sacrifices. Not the mind only, and not on Sunday only: the body, with its hours and appetites and hands. Do not be conformed to this age, he says, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then he turns at once to the church as one body with many gifts, so that renewal is never a private project.

The rest of the chapter is love made specific. Love without pretending, honour one another, share with the saints in need, practise hospitality. Bless those who persecute you. Do not repay evil for evil, and leave vengeance to God. The chapter ends, “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21). That is not a command to stay where you are being harmed, and the notes say so plainly.

open.label: Romans 12, passage by passage
open.why: Living sacrifices, renewed minds, one body with many gifts, sincere love and overcoming evil with good, each explained in plain words.

also.label: The church in the Study Bible
also.why: What Scripture means by the church as one body with many members, the picture Paul uses in the middle of this chapter.

also.label: Key words of the Bible
also.why: Look up mercy, love and the other words this chapter leans on, and see how the whole Bible uses them.

sessions.question: Paul says to offer your body as a living sacrifice. Which part of your ordinary day have you kept back from God?
sessions.do: Choose one line from Romans 12:9-21 that you find hardest. Write it on a card, carry it for a week, and note each time it applied to something that happened.

verse.text: Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.

care: Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who is someone whose ordinary kindness has shaped you more than any sermon?
discuss: Why do you think Paul spends eleven chapters on what God has done before he says what we should do?
What does it look like in your setting to be conformed to the pattern of this age without noticing?
Overcome evil with good has been misused to keep people in harm. How do you hold the command and the warning together?
group.pray: Offer to God in your own words the coming week, hours and body and work, and pray for anyone in the group who has an enemy to bless.

sessions.title: Rulers, love, and the coming day
teaching: Paul tells the church in Rome to submit to the governing authorities, pay taxes and give respect, because rulers hold their authority from God. He describes government as it is meant to work, a terror to bad conduct and not to good. He does not say rulers may command anything. When the apostles were forbidden to preach, they said they must obey God rather than men, and Revelation pictures Rome's power turned against the church as a beast. This passage has been misused to defend slavery and tyranny, and the notes reject that use under every government.

Christians differ on when disobedience is right and on the state's sword, with pacifists on one side and the just war tradition, from Augustine to Aquinas, on the other; the notes take no side, and Romans names no party. Then Paul names the one debt that stays, to love one another. The night is nearly over. In 386 Augustine read the chapter's last lines in a garden in Milan, and his life turned on them.

open.label: Romans 13, passage by passage
open.why: The governing authorities, the debt of love and the night nearly over, with how the passage has been used and misused set out plainly.

also.label: Does Romans 13 mean obeying every government?
also.why: What Paul said about rulers in the Rome of Nero's early years, what he did not say, and how the passage has been bent.

also.label: Should a Christian follow a political party?
also.why: The question this chapter is so often recruited to answer, taken up with the same measure for the right and the left.

also.label: The state in the Study Bible
also.why: What the whole Bible says about rulers, from Joseph in Egypt to Revelation, so that Romans 13 is not read alone.

sessions.question: Paul tells the church to honour rulers and to owe no one anything but love. Which of those two is harder for you right now?
sessions.do: Read Romans 13:1-7 and then Acts 5:27-29 and Revelation 13:1-8. Write down what each passage adds to the other two.

verse.text: Be indebted to no one, except to one another in love. For he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.

group.open: What did you learn as a child about how to treat people in authority?
discuss: How has this chapter been used to silence Christians under injustice, and why do the notes reject that use?
State the pacifist view and the just war view as their holders would. What does each think the other forgets?
Paul moves from taxes to love to the coming day. What holds the chapter together?
group.pray: Pray for those who govern where you live, whatever their party, and ask for the courage to obey God when that and obeying men are not the same.

sessions.title: The weak and the strong
teaching: The church in Rome was divided over food and days. Some ate only vegetables, likely to avoid meat that might have been offered to idols or was not kosher, and kept certain days holy. Others ate anything and treated every day alike. Paul calls the first group weak in faith and counts himself among the strong, and then spends the whole chapter protecting the weak. The one who eats must not despise the one who abstains, and the one who abstains must not judge the one who eats.

Each will give an account to God, not to the other. “For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17). The strong may be right about the food and still wrong to use their freedom in a way that destroys a brother. This is how a church lives with questions the gospel does not settle, by refusing both contempt and judgment.

open.label: Romans 14, passage by passage
open.why: The weak and the strong, food and holy days, and the warning not to destroy the work of God over food, explained in plain words.

also.label: The Christian traditions
also.why: How the families of churches differ in practice and conviction, a place to practise Paul's rule of no contempt and no judgment.

also.label: Themes of the Bible
also.why: Follow the kingdom of God through the books that speak of it, and see why Paul says it is not about eating and drinking.

sessions.question: Paul says the strong must not despise and the weak must not judge. Which are you more tempted to do, and toward whom?
sessions.do: Think of one Christian practice you are free about and another believer is not. This week, give up your freedom in that matter once, for their sake, without telling them.

verse.text: For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.

group.open: What is a disagreement among Christians you know that turned out to matter less than it seemed?
discuss: Paul counts himself among the strong and spends the chapter defending the weak. Why?
What questions in today's church work like food and days did in Rome, and which do not?
When does using your freedom become a way of despising someone else?
group.pray: Pray for a believer you disagree with on a second-order matter, by name, and ask that both of you would seek righteousness, peace and joy.

sessions.title: Accept one another, and the road to Spain
teaching: Paul closes his argument with the example behind it all: Christ did not please himself. So the strong bear with the weak, and the whole church is told, “Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you, in order to bring glory to God” (Romans 15:7). Then he strings together verses from the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms, all about the Gentiles praising God with Israel. The letter's long argument about Jew and Gentile ends in a single choir.

Then Paul explains himself. He has preached from Jerusalem round to Illyricum, and now he plans to carry a gift from the Gentile churches of Greece to the poor believers in Jerusalem, then visit Rome on the way to Spain. He asks them to pray that he will be rescued from unbelievers in Judea. Acts tells what happened next: he was arrested in Jerusalem and came to Rome in chains.

open.label: Romans 15, passage by passage
open.why: Christ who did not please himself, the Gentiles praising God, Paul's priestly service and his plans for Jerusalem, Rome and Spain.

also.label: Paul's travels
also.why: The cities Paul names in this chapter on a map, from Jerusalem round to Illyricum, and the road he hoped would take him on to Spain.

also.label: The Bible's timeline
also.why: Where Romans falls among Paul's letters and travels, and how its writing in Corinth fits with his last visit to Jerusalem.

also.label: Did Paul invent Christianity?
also.why: The strongest form of the claim that Paul made a new religion out of Jesus, and the evidence on the other side, set out fairly.

sessions.question: Paul says to accept one another as Christ accepted you. Whom have you accepted only on your own terms?
sessions.do: Read Romans 15:22-33 and then Acts 21:17-36. Write down what Paul asked the Romans to pray for and what happened, and how you would have prayed if you were them.

verse.text: Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace as you believe in Him, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.

group.open: What plan have you made that went somewhere you did not expect?
discuss: Paul ends his argument with Jews and Gentiles praising God together. Why is unity the climax of a letter about justification?
Paul carried money from Gentile churches to poor Jewish believers. What did that gift say that words could not?
Paul's prayer request was answered, though not as he pictured. How do you read his prayer in the light of Acts?
group.pray: Pray for a church unlike yours, in your town or far away, and ask the God of hope to fill each person in the group with joy and peace.

sessions.title: A church of names
teaching: The greatest argument in the New Testament ends with a list of names. Paul commends Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae, the port of Corinth, who most likely carried the letter to Rome. He greets Prisca and Aquila, who risked their necks for him and have a church in their house, and Andronicus and Junia, who were in Christ before he was. Readers differ on whether Junia was counted among the apostles or well known to them, and on what Phoebe's title meant; the notes set out both, and the question of office stays open.

Jews and Gentiles, men and women, slaves and free are named side by side. Tertius, who wrote the letter down, adds his own greeting. Romans does not end with a summary of justification. It ends with people who were justified, known by name, and with a promise that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under their feet. The gospel of chapters 1 to 11 was always meant to make a household like this one.

open.label: Romans 16, passage by passage
open.why: Phoebe, a church of names, a final warning and promise, greetings from Corinth and the doxology, each explained in plain words.

also.label: The first Christians
also.why: The church of these names, from Pentecost to the generation after the apostles, and what it cost them to be known as Christians.

also.label: The Apostles' Creed
also.why: The oldest summary of the faith still in use, with notes on each line, which gathers what Romans argues into words a whole church can say.

also.label: The Academy's tracks
also.why: Every track on the site, including What Christians Believe, which begins with the Apostles' Creed and takes up line by line the faith Romans argued.

sessions.question: Paul ends his greatest letter with a list of friends. Whose name would be on your list, and does anyone have yours on theirs?
sessions.do: Write a short note this week to someone who has served you in the faith, as Paul did, naming what they did. Then go back to Romans 1 and read the first chapter again in the light of the last.

verse.text: The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

group.open: Which of these sixteen sessions will you remember longest, and why?
discuss: Why might it matter that the letter ends with names rather than with a summary of its argument?
Readers differ on Junia and Phoebe. How can a group hold that question open and still honour both women?
Looking back over the whole letter, what does Romans say is wrong with us, and what has God done about it?
group.pray: Give thanks by name for each person in the group, and for those who first brought the gospel to you, and ask that your church would be a household like the one in Rome.
